readerTitle: Britannica wasn't beaten by a better encyclopedia
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Encyclopaedia Britannica, Microsoft Encarta, Wikipedia) + 실제 연구 (Nature 2005 비교) + 가상 적용 (집수리 서비스)
insight: 기술은 1등 제품보다 더 좋은 제품을 만들기보다 '충분히 좋은' 제품을 전혀 다른 비용 구조로 만들게 한다. 그때 살아남는 길은 여전히 희소한 것을 파는 것이다.
misconception: 품질이 더 좋으면 무료 경쟁자에게 지지 않는다. 또는 디지털로 옮기기만 하면 살아남는다.

sources.text: Evans, P. & Wurster, T. S. (1997). Strategy and the New Economics of Information. Harvard Business Review. (Blown to Bits, 2000에도 Britannica 사례 수록)
Giles, J. (2005). Internet encyclopaedias go head to head. Nature 438, 900–901.
Bosman, J. (2012, March 13). After 244 Years, Encyclopaedia Britannica Stops the Presses. The New York Times.
Microsoft announcement on discontinuing MSN Encarta (2009)
Wikimedia Foundation, history of Wikipedia (launched January 2001)

factChecks.note: Britannica 초판 1768년 에든버러 발행, 2012년 3월 인쇄판 중단 발표(마지막 인쇄판은 2010년판 32권)를 NYT 기사와 Britannica 공식 자료로 확인하세요.
인쇄판 세트 가격을 "well over a thousand dollars"로 적었습니다. 1990년대 가격은 자료마다 다르며 2010년판은 약 $1,395로 보도되었습니다. 정확한 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
Britannica가 CD-ROM을 세트에 끼워 주거나 단독으로는 높은 가격에 팔았다는 내용은 Evans & Wurster(1997)의 설명에 근거합니다. 카드에서 출처를 밝혔습니다. 구체 금액은 넣지 않았습니다.
방문판매 조직 해체 시점은 1996년 무렵으로 알려져 있으나 카드에는 시점 없이 "was dismantled"로만 적었습니다. 확인 후 연도를 추가할 수 있습니다.
Encarta 출시 1993년, Microsoft의 서비스 종료 2009년을 확인하세요. Wikipedia 출시 2001년 1월.

Nature 2005 연구: 과학 기사 42편 비교, 심각한 오류는 양쪽 각 4건, 사실 오류·누락·오해 소지 표현은 Wikipedia 162건 vs Britannica 123건(기사당 약 4건 vs 3건). 카드에는 수치 없이 "only somewhat less accurate on average"로 적었습니다. Britannica는 2006년 방법론을 공식 반박했습니다.
Britannica가 인쇄 중단 후 온라인 구독과 교육용 상품(학교·도서관)으로 옮겼다는 내용은 일반적으로 보도된 범위로만 적었습니다. 매출·수익 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Britannica wasn't beaten by a better encyclopedia
body: Encyclopaedia Britannica was first published in Edinburgh in 1768. For generations, families bought the full set from salespeople who came to the door.
In 2012, it announced it would stop printing. Its strongest rival was written by unpaid volunteers and cost readers nothing.

image.label: A tall row of leather-bound encyclopedia volumes beside a glowing laptop
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 무겁고 두꺼운 가죽 장정 백과사전 세트가 책장에 줄지어 있고, 오른쪽에 작은 노트북 화면이 밝게 빛남. 실제 Britannica·Wikipedia 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A disc threatens your bookshelf.
body: It's the early 1990s and you run Britannica. Your sets cost families well over a thousand dollars, and a large commissioned sales force sells them door to door.
Rivals now fit a whole encyclopedia on one CD-ROM for a small fraction of that price, often packaged with new home computers. What do you do?

options.text: Make a CD-ROM, but price it high so it doesn't undercut the sets or the sales force
options.feedback: It protects this year's revenue and keeps your salespeople on side. But customers are already comparing you with cheap discs, and a high price sends them to your rivals.

options.text: Sell a cheap disc and start shrinking the print business yourself
options.feedback: You give up high-margin sets and the sales force sooner. In return you keep customers and your name while the market moves.

options.text: Cut the price of print sets and add a free disc
options.feedback: It slows the loss, but you keep the printing and sales costs your rivals don't have. The gap in price never fully closes.

cards.title: Britannica protected the old business.
body: In Evans and Wurster's widely cited account, Britannica first tried to shield print. The CD-ROM came with a set, or at a high price on its own.

It didn't work. Microsoft's Encarta, launched in 1993, was cheap and good enough for homework. Britannica's print sales fell steeply through the 1990s, and its door-to-door sales force was dismantled.
Then in 2001 came **Wikipedia**: free, online, and written by anyone.

cards.title: Good enough, at a different cost
body: New technology rarely beats a leader by making a better version of its product. More often it lets a rival make a **good-enough** version at a completely different cost.

Britannica paid experts, editors, printers and salespeople. Encarta's extra copies cost almost nothing. Wikipedia's writers weren't paid at all. Once a free option did the job for most customers, Britannica's quality edge mattered only to the few who needed it.

image.label: Three cost stacks: print set, CD-ROM, volunteer-written website
image.brief: 세 개의 비용 막대 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Print set" 막대는 "Experts", "Printing", "Salespeople" 층으로 높게, 가운데 "CD-ROM"은 낮게, 오른쪽 "Volunteer website"는 거의 바닥 높이. 수치 없이 높이만으로 차이를 표현. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How good was good enough?
body: In 2005 the journal *Nature* had experts review science articles from both encyclopedias without saying which was which. It found errors in both, with Wikipedia only somewhat less accurate on average.

Britannica strongly disputed the method. But for most readers the debate missed the point. A free encyclopedia that was close enough, constantly updated and one click away won the everyday job of looking something up.

cards.title: From owning facts to vouching for them.
body: Britannica didn't disappear. It stopped printing and turned to online subscriptions and learning products, especially for schools and libraries.

Those customers still pay for something free alternatives struggle to promise: content checked by named editors that teachers can rely on. The value moved from owning the information to **vouching for it**.
cards.softwareNote: Paid software tools face this when a free or open-source alternative becomes good enough. Companies that survive often charge for what stays scarce: hosting, security, support or guarantees.

cards.title: Free and digital doesn't always win.
body: Encarta was digital and cheap, yet Microsoft shut it down in 2009. Going digital wasn't enough once an even cheaper model arrived.

And good enough depends on the job. Where an error is costly, as with medical, legal or safety information, customers still pay for verified sources. Don't assume your quality edge is worthless. Find out exactly who still needs it.

cards.title: Now it's a home-repair business.
body: You run a handyman service. Free online videos now teach people to fix dripping taps, hang shelves and patch walls. Calls for small jobs are falling.

options.text: Lower prices on small jobs to win them back
options.feedback: You may keep a few customers, but you're fighting free on price. The videos will only get better, and your margins get thinner.

options.text: Focus on jobs where mistakes are costly, like wiring and leaks, and back the work with a guarantee
options.feedback: You give up easy jobs, but you sell what a video can't: skill, accountability and a promise if something goes wrong.

options.text: Post your own free how-to videos
options.feedback: It builds trust and may bring in jobs viewers can't finish. On its own, though, it gives away small jobs without a plan for what you'll sell instead.

cards.title: When good enough becomes free, sell what's still scarce.
body: Ask which customers would switch to a free, good-enough option, and what the rest still pay for.
**Try it today:** name the cheapest alternative a customer could use instead of you. Write down the one thing you offer that it can't.
